seeded_from: Three delivered BMad projects, re-derived 2026-09-09. EPP carries the only per-story measured record — docs/reference/phase-1-per-feature-estimate.csv — and it is what the size bands are fitted to. memorial-healthcare and easyterms carry per-role totals only, and are used to check the fit rather than to make it.
calibration_status: THREE ANCHORS AT PROJECT LEVEL, ONE AT STORY LEVEL (n=3 / n=1). Per-role actuals: EPP epics 1-9 = 690 h (dev 300 / architect 110 / BA 100 / UX 100 / QA 40 / DevOps 40) over 7 weeks; memorial-healthcare epics 1-9.7 = 360 h (dev 140 / architect 60 / BA 80 / UX 80, no QA, no DevOps) over 3.5 weeks; easyterms epics 1-5+8 = 240 h (dev 160 / architect 80, no other role staffed) over 5 weeks. ONLY EPP recorded effort per story, so the size bands rest on it alone; the other two can falsify the fit at project level and do not contribute to it. Say n=3 for the shape and n=1 for the bands whenever a client asks how these numbers were arrived at. SUPERSEDES the 540 h EPP figure the 2.x model was fitted to: the same scope is now recorded at 690 h (architect +80, BA +60, dev +20, DevOps +10, UX -20), so every 2.x coefficient carrying '540 h actual' was fitted 22% low against its own anchor.

projects.name: EPP (myEPP) epics 1-9
projects.per_story_record: docs/reference/phase-1-per-feature-estimate.csv — every story weighted XS=1..XL=5; epics 1-7 measured at 206 points / 240 dev h = 1.165 h per point, re-checked independently on Phase 2.1 at 75 points / 88 dev h = 1.173 h per point (0.7% apart).

calibration_history.why: The 2.x model priced a manual-equivalent baseline divided by a compressibility factor. NEITHER QUANTITY WAS RECORDED ON ANY OF THE THREE PROJECTS — what every one of them recorded is delivered hours. The frame therefore moves: size_bands now hold delivered hours, and the manual-equivalent is derived from them for the client narrative and consumed by nothing. Three measured results drove the rebuild. (1) The band spread is 4.8x, not 90x: EPP's own 1-5 point scale runs 1.2 h to 5.8 h of dev time per story, where the 2.x bands ran 1 h to 90 h of manual baseline. (2) review_tier does not move a story's delivered hours: sensitive stories average 3.24 points against routine 3.08 — 1.05x — and 1.06x once provider-touching stories are excluded, where 2.x priced the tier at a 3.5x swing on the review component. (3) What DOES move them is the provider: a money rail carries +0.75 points over what its surface count predicts, an external IdP +0.73, native/device +0.41, and a pure in-app story -0.07. That is the console work, the credentials and the provider round-trips, and it does not scale with how big the story is — so it is priced as an additive premium, not as a band.

Retained so a reader can tell which coefficients were fitted to which figure. The 2.x model fitted size_bands, review_rate, clarity, qa and role_weights against 540 h actual (dev 280 / UX 120 / QA 40 / BA 40 / DevOps 30 / architect 30). The same scope is now recorded at 690 h. Nothing in the 2.x fit survives into 3.0 unchanged.

_reading_this_file: Each coefficient is a three-point estimate (lo / likely / hi) plus a 'why' saying what it encodes. Change a value by editing it here — nothing in the skill hardcodes a number. Every estimate snapshots this whole file into its ledger entry, so a later change never rewrites the past.

size_bands._what: Delivered hours for one STORY, across every role billed to story work (dev, UX, BA's specification share, DevOps). NOT a manual-equivalent baseline, and NOT divided by anything: the 2.x model priced manual_baseline / compressibility, and neither of those was ever measured on a delivered project. These are. `measured_dev_h` on each band is EPP's own recorded figure — its 1-5 complexity scale at 1.165 h of DEV time per point — and `likely` is that figure grossed up by 1.32 to cover the other roles that are billed to a story. The gross-up is the one fitted number here; the shape is measured. THE SPREAD IS 4.8x, XS to XL. The 2.x bands ran 1 h to 90 h, an 18-fold wider spread, and that is where the sizing bias came from: a one-band error moved a story's cost 3.0x under 2.x against the 1.34x the delivered record shows.

_anchor.source: EPP epics 1-9: docs/reference/phase-1-per-feature-estimate.csv weights all 75 stories on a 1-5 scale and reconciles to the measured total. Epics 1-7: 63 stories, 206 points, 240 dev h = 1.165 h/point. Re-run independently on Phase 2.1 (23 stories, 75 points, 88 dev h): 1.173 h/point, 0.7% apart, with mean points/story 3.27 vs 3.26. Applying the scale across epics 1-9 gives 237 points -> 276 h against the 300 h actual.
_anchor.h_per_point_dev_cross_project: EPP 1.165 (measured). memorial-healthcare 0.866 and easyterms 0.623 (BRIDGED, not measured: their stories were mapped onto this scale by files-touched using EPP's own files->points mapping, which carries a 1.09-point mean error per story and lands within 4% in aggregate). The 1.9x spread is granularity: the bridged mix puts 88 of memorial-healthcare's stories at 1 point and 27 of easyterms' at 5. This model is fitted to the EPP end of that range and will therefore run HIGH against a finely-sliced inventory. check_granularity is what catches that.
_anchor.surfaces_per_story_why: MEASURED on EPP's 75 delivered stories, using this module's five-surface taxonomy. It is the one sizing signal an extraction cannot satisfy by re-slicing, and it separates the three anchors where nothing else does: EPP 2.29, memorial-healthcare 1.25, easyterms 1.12 — while hours per surface-touch stay inside 1.74x (4.01 / 2.31 / 2.76) against a 3.2x spread on hours per story. check_granularity compares an inventory against it and reports which way the estimate will be wrong.
_anchor.baseline_per_story_h_why: The M band, i.e. what a median story costs. Kept because inventory-check's older ratio reads it — but note it divides by the story count, which the extraction itself chooses, so it can always be satisfied by re-slicing. surfaces_per_story is the check that cannot.
_anchor.baseline_per_source_line_h_why: For a row-shaped source, where each story absorbs several rows of the client's own document. Derived, not measured directly: the anchor's median story is M at 4.6 h and carries 8 acceptance criteria, so 0.58 h per stated requirement. The weakest of the three ratios and the one to trust least — the denominator is the extraction's own citation policy, so it can be moved at will. It is kept because a wildly different figure still means something; surfaces_per_story is the check that cannot be gamed.
_anchor.why: The shape a band assignment is compared against, never a rule it must obey — and NOT a target to move toward. The 2.x model claimed XS 0%, S 11%, M 64%, L 25%, XL 0%, and the classification guide told the classifier to expect 64% M before it judged anything. The measured record is above: M is 45%, L is 31%, and BOTH XS AND XL EXIST. An inventory at 37% L is inside a band-and-a-half of the anchor, not three times over it. Read this to notice a shape you did not intend, then argue with it.
_anchor.not_the_discriminator: Acceptance-criterion count does not separate the bands. Median ACs by band across EPP's 75 stories run 5 / 7 / 8.5 / 8 / 12 — M and L are indistinguishable. What does separate them is the number of distinct surfaces the story touches (median 1 / 2 / 3 / 3 / 4) plus whether it introduces a capability the codebase does not have.
_anchor.review_tier_is_not_size: MEASURED, and it is the finding that most changes how these bands should be read: EPP's sensitive stories average 3.24 points against routine 3.08 — 1.05x — and 1.06x with every provider-touching story excluded. Criticality does not make a story bigger. It is priced in review_tier, at a multiplier that now reflects that.
_anchor.gross_up_why: 1.32. The measured 1.165 h/point is DEV time; a story also carries UX, the BA's specification share and DevOps. Fitted — the only fitted number in this block — by minimising relative error across EPP's five staffed non-DevOps role totals (dev 300 / UX 100 / BA 100 / QA 40 / architect 110), which lands them at 1.05x / 1.01x / 0.97x / 0.98x / 0.77x. n=1: EPP is the only anchor that staffed all six roles. DevOps is outside the fit on purpose — its 40 h went on pipelines and environments, which are standing_work and are in no story list.

XS.why: A cleanup batch, a one-line projection fix, one field on a form that already exists
exemplars: EPP 4.0 'Pre-Epic-4 hardening' — small carry-over cleanup batch; no feature surface (1 pt)
EPP 9.8 'Public card buyable ticket availability' — one-line projection fix (1 pt)
2.7% of the anchor's delivered stories. The 2.x model asserted that none of them was XS and warned on every XS tag; two of them were, and the warning was pushing real work up a band.

S.why: A read-only projection over data that exists, a second terminal state on a gate already built, a thin late add-on reusing a path that already runs
exemplars: EPP 1.14 'Suspended / deactivated member state' — two terminal states reusing the existing gate (2 pts)
EPP 2.11 'Member registration status & history' — read-only projection over existing data (2 pts)
EPP 4.6 'Event hub' — composition over already-built modules, little net-new backend (2 pts)
EPP 2.16 'Admin invite / non-member registration' — reuses the registration path, no net-new schema (2 pts)

M.why: The median story: two or three surfaces, real rules of its own, nothing the codebase has not done before
exemplars: EPP 1.1 'Monorepo scaffold & shared contracts' — multi-surface, no domain logic (3 pts)
EPP 2.7 'Event catalog — browse, search, filter' — query/filter/pagination projection (3 pts)
EPP 1.11 'Member approval / rejection & role administration' — workflow, role transitions, notification side-effects (3 pts)
EPP 7.2 'German language pack' — high translation volume, low structural risk (3 pts)
not_exemplars: Not S because a second entity still needs its own rules, its own screens and its own tests

Not L for being central: EPP 2.1 'Staff event create/edit', the largest entity in the model, is L because it is the epic's spine — but 2.8 'Event detail page', a composed read over five sub-entities, is M. Reach is review_tier's business.

L.why: Four surfaces, or the first of its kind in this codebase: a protocol, a transport, an external system, or a foundation everything after it is built on
exemplars: EPP 1.5 'Login / logout & persistent session' — DB, API, Redis and Member Web; refresh-token rotation in Redis Lua (4 pts)
EPP 1.7 'Microsoft Entra SSO' — external IdP, OIDC round-trip, account linking (4 pts)
EPP 4.3 '1-to-1 event chat' — the first realtime transport: Socket.IO gateway plus Redis adapter (4 pts)
EPP 2.6 'Per-event custom registration fields' — a schema-driven form builder rendering and validating on both sides (4 pts)
EPP 5.2 'QR scan check-in (staff, native)' — native camera behind a capability check (4 pts)
not_exemplars: Not CRUD over one entity, however central the entity is
Not a list plus its detail view, however many features read from it
Not a derived read the whole product depends on — size it as the query it is

XL.why: A subsystem tracked as one row. Rare and real: 4% of the anchor, and every one of them was a third-party lifecycle the app had to hold state against
exemplars: EPP 3.3 'Paid recurring membership' — Stripe Subscriptions, invoice.paid webhook lifecycle, credit grant per invoice (5 pts)
EPP 3.4 'Paid event checkout, credits as discount' — credit debit and access grant as ONE atomic operation; its epic retro records four CRITICAL money/race bugs found in this story alone (5 pts)
EPP 6.1 'One-way Zoho CRM sync' — largest spec in Phase 1: field mapping across four objects, queue and worker (5 pts)
XL is still a signal to look for a split, and est-estimate prices a narrowing question for each one — but it is NOT an error. The 2.x model asserted the anchor left none XL; three of them were.

manual_effort_premium._what: Additive hours for work whose cost is NOT the code. Console clicking, credentials, provider dashboards, store review, back-and-forth with someone else's support desk, and verification an agent cannot perform. It is added to the story AFTER the band and BEFORE the multipliers, because it does not scale with how big the story is — a Stripe account is the same amount of console work whether it backs one checkout or three. MEASURED as the residual over what a story's surface count alone predicts, across EPP's 75 weighted stories. Several premiums can apply to one story; they sum. Tag a story with the `manual_effort` array in classification.json; an absent or empty array is zero.
manual_effort_premium._how_it_was_measured: For each of EPP's 75 stories, the expected point weight was taken as the mean weight of every story with the same surface count, and the residual is the story's actual weight minus that. Grouping the residuals: money rail +0.75 (n=4), external IdP +0.73 (n=1), native/device +0.41 (n=4), any third-party provider +0.18 (n=24), pure in-app with no provider -0.07 (n=49). The last row is the control: stories that touch nothing external sit on the line.

money_rail.why: A payment or billing provider is integrated: account and product setup, webhook endpoints and signing secrets, test-mode reconciliation, and the idempotency work that money forces. Two of the anchor's three XL stories are the Stripe ones, and epic 3's retro records four CRITICAL money/race bugs found in story 3.4 alone.

external_idp.why: An external identity provider is configured: app registration, redirect URIs, client secrets, tenant consent, and a round-trip that can only be proven against the real provider.
external_idp.evidence: EPP 1.7 Microsoft Entra SSO, residual +0.73 pts (n=1) — the weakest cell in this block

native_release.why: A device build or a store channel: signing identities, provisioning profiles, native toolchain linkage, and verification that only runs on real hardware. EPP's epic-5 retro names the mechanism outright — 'native-build verification is invisible to the planning loop' — after an iOS SPM-to-CocoaPods linkage could not be resolved headlessly.
native_release.evidence: EPP 5.1.5 and 5.2, mean residual +0.41 pts (n=4). Both sit at 4 points on only TWO surfaces — the highest points-per-surface ratio in the project.

provisioning.why: Real environments, credentials, DNS and TLS against a live cloud account. UNPRICED, DELIBERATELY, AND FLAGGED: none of the three anchors paid for it. EPP's Infra-tagged stories score 0.51 points BELOW prediction because 7.5 is marked 'seams only, IaC deferred'; its epic-6 and epic-7 retros say 'no AWS resource was provisioned' and that SES was 'still in sandbox'; memorial-healthcare 1.4 ships CI with 'placeholder steps for EC2 deployment'. A story carrying this trigger gets an open question, not a number, until one project that actually reached production reports actuals.
provisioning.evidence: Negative: EPP Infra residual -0.51 pts (n=2), and all three projects deferred IaC

compressibility._what: REPORTED ONLY — nothing is divided by this any more. In 2.x it was the divisor that turned a manual-equivalent baseline into build hours; the baseline was never measured on any delivered project, so the division was arithmetic over a construct. It now runs the other way: manual_equivalent = delivered_hours x compressibility, computed so the client narrative survives, and consumed by no downstream figure. If it is wrong, the estimate is unaffected and only the 'this would have cost X by hand' sentence moves. EVIDENCE IS ONE SENTENCE: EPP's own effort assessment states its delivered velocity is 'AI-assisted (BMAD + Claude Code) ... roughly 8-10x traditional hand-coding' and that its first-pass sizes assuming traditional velocity 'were ~8x too high'. Nobody estimated any of these three projects manually, so the level is an assertion and the consistency across the three is inferred. Confidence 3/10 on the level, 6/10 on the order.

high.why: CRUD, greenfield screens, scaffolding, well-documented APIs, tests, docs, config

medium.why: Conventional business logic, common integrations, standard mobile screens

low.why: Undocumented legacy, client-proprietary systems, bespoke algorithms, dirty-data migration, pixel-level craft — the effort is discovery, and discovery does not compress

none.why: Workshops, approvals, compliance sign-off, third-party lead times — no code is the deliverable

review_tier._what: A multiplier on the story's delivered hours, and it is SMALL — this is the coefficient the rebuild changed most. MEASURED on EPP: sensitive stories average 3.24 points against routine 3.08, a ratio of 1.05x, and 1.06x once every provider-touching story is excluded so the money premium cannot flatter it. The 2.x model priced the tier at 0.04 / 0.17 / 0.30 of a manual baseline — a 3.5x swing on the review component and roughly 1.9x on a story's total. Criticality is real and it is expensive in consequences; under this delivery model, with a fresh-context agent review pass per story, it is NOT expensive in hours. What IS expensive is the provider behind the sensitive work, and that is priced in manual_effort_premium. The tier still decides WHO reviews (see role_weights.review) and still shifts the phase decomposition toward review; it barely moves the total. `critical` is the exception and it is a JUDGEMENT, not a measurement: none of the three anchors carried an external compliance sign-off, so the 1.25 below is a hypothesis about work they did not contain. Confidence: sensitive 7/10 (measured, n=75 stories), critical 2/10.

routine.why: Delegate the feature whole; spot-review DB migrations, tests, CI/CD

sensitive.why: Money, personal data, authentication and authorization: read line by line before anyone signs their name to it. MEASURED at 1.05x of a routine story's hours — the reading is more careful, not longer.

critical.why: Regulated data, irreversible financial effects, safety: line-by-line plus an external or compliance sign-off that runs on someone else's calendar. UNMEASURED — no anchor had one.

clarity._what: How precisely the source specifies the story. Three separate effects, kept separate on purpose: `multiplier` moves the story's hours, `spec_share_adjust`/`rework_share_adjust` move where those hours are reported in the phase table, and `band_multiplier` widens the story's own interval around its likely value. UNMEASURED: none of the three anchors recorded hours by phase, only by role, so there is nothing to fit the level against — the ORDERING is the claim, and it is the one the module argues for. Under BMad, ambiguity is not resolved by a developer stopping to ask; it gets confidently implemented, reviewed, and rebuilt. The multipliers are deliberately modest against 2.x, whose spec and rework rates could add more to a story than its own build. Confidence 2/10 on the level, 6/10 on the ordering. BAND: without band_multiplier the spread ran BACKWARDS — a real inventory produced hi/lo of 6.32 at high clarity against 5.52 at low, because scalar multiples of an interval are proportionally tight and adding more of them pulled the ratio down. A vague story read as the more certain one.

high.band_multiplier_why: Acceptance criteria present, data model implied, edge cases named — the interval the band already implies needs no widening
high.why: Acceptance criteria present, data model implied, edge cases named

medium.band_multiplier_why: Clear in prose, intent unambiguous, details absent. The details are where the hours hide, so the spread widens by an exponent on hi/lo
medium.why: Clear in prose, intent unambiguous, details absent

low.band_multiplier_why: A line in a transcript, or inferred from context. What is being built is genuinely not yet known, and a narrow band here would be false precision
low.why: A line in a transcript, or inferred from context

novelty_rework_multiplier._what: New to the team, or genuinely uncommon. In 2.x this multiplied the rework component only, at 1.5x; with rework now a share of the story rather than an addition to it, the same 1.5 would have been a 50% uplift on the whole story, which no anchor supports. Set at 1.15 on the total and 1.6 on the rework share. UNMEASURED — none of the three projects recorded which stories were novel to the team.

standard.why: The team has built something of this shape before

novel.why: New to the team or genuinely uncommon. Novelty drives loops rather than build effort — the first attempt at an unfamiliar shape rarely converges in one pass

component_shares._what: How a story's delivered hours DIVIDE across the four phases. A decomposition, not a computation: the story total is set by the band, the premium and the multipliers, and these shares only decide where those hours are reported and which role_weights table splits them. They always sum to 1, so moving a share can never change a story's cost. EXPLICITLY A HYPOTHESIS. All three anchors recorded hours by ROLE and never by PHASE, so there is nothing here to fit against. It is stated as numbers rather than left implicit so that a reader can see the claim and a future project can falsify it. Confidence 2/10. Adjustments from review_tier, clarity and novelty are applied multiplicatively to the base and then renormalised: a vague sensitive story reports roughly 37% build against a routine specified one's 60%.
component_shares._raise_confidence_by: One project that time-tracks a story to build / specify / review / rework rather than to a role.

team_profiles._what: Modifiers on the judgement-heavy components only — spec, review and rework. build is left alone because the agent writes the code either way. UNMEASURED: all three anchors ran the same team shape and none of them recorded seniority against hours, so these are the 2.x values carried forward as assertions. Confidence 2/10. Raise it by delivering one project with a materially different team.

senior-heavy.why: Sharper specs, faster sensitive-tier review, fewer loops to converge

balanced.why: The baseline the other profiles are relative to

junior-heavy.why: Review is slower and less reliable, and more loops are needed — the cost lands hardest where BMad concentrates human effort

new-to-bmad.why: A learning-curve modifier independent of seniority. Decays over the first few projects; est-calibrate should retire it per team once actuals show it has

planning._what: The BMad planning pipeline. Priced per artefact written, so it is the ONE place where slicing a story in two genuinely costs more: two stories get two story files and two reviews. Everything else in this model is invariant to slicing, and split_factor exists to keep that distinction honest.
planning.features_per_epic_why: Fallback only, for an inventory whose stories carry no epic. Keyed to PLANNED granularity, which is what an inventory holds: EPP planned 50 stories over 8 epics (6.3), memorial-healthcare 63 over 9 (7.0), easyterms 50 over 6 (8.3). The delivered figures are higher (8.4 / 8.3 / 13.4) because stories were split during delivery, and using them here would count epics against a story total that has not been split yet. The 2.x value of 8 sat between the two.
planning.split_factor_why: How many story artefacts get written per story in the inventory. MEASURED on all three: EPP 50 planned stories were delivered as 76 (1.52x), memorial-healthcare 63 as 125 (1.98x), easyterms 50 as 78 (1.56x). This is DECOMPOSITION, NOT SCOPE GROWTH — a story that turned out too big was split, the scope did not change, and the delivered hours above already include the result. It is applied to planning ONLY, because planning is the only component priced per artefact. Applying it to build would bill the same work twice. It replaces 2.x's stories_per_feature, which keyed the same idea off the size band and so claimed that big stories split and small ones do not; the record shows splitting is a property of the project, not of the band. Worth 1.5% of EPP's total and 7% of memorial-healthcare's. Confidence 6/10.

agent_hours._what: Human time steering the BMad workflow that authors each artefact — already compressed, since the agent drafts.

review_hours._what: Human time READING every planning artefact, end to end, no exceptions. Bands are deliberately tight — tighter than anything else in this model — because this is the one component the company performs identically on every project. It is reading at a known rate over a known volume, so the uncertainty is in the volume, not the rate. Report it with a visibly narrower range: it is the part of the number that can be defended hardest, and its tightness is the evidence for that claim rather than a rhetorical flourish.

documents_by_granularity.why: A whole project pays the full planning pipeline once. An epic inside a running project inherits the brief and UX and pays only for its own requirements and technical design. A sprint or single feature pays neither — the planning artefacts already exist.

architect._what: The architect is priced as SETUP PLUS A WEEKLY RATE, not as a share of anything. This is the best-evidenced coefficient in the model: all three delivered projects fit the same formula exactly, and it was stated independently of the totals rather than fitted to them. EPP 40 h setup + 7 weeks x 10 = 110. memorial-healthcare 30 + 3 x 10 = 60. easyterms 30 + 5 x 10 = 80. The 2.x model had no architect component at all: the hours fell out of role_weights on planning_agent (0.35), planning_review (0.35) and overhead (0.40), every one of which scales with story and epic count. On a 371-story inventory that produced 3x the anchored setup; on a 76-story one it would have produced far less. Setup does not scale with the backlog, and support scales with the calendar. Confidence 9/10.
architect.setup_h_why: Standing the project up: repository and environment decisions, the architecture artefact, the conventions every later story inherits. Recorded at 30 h on two projects and 40 h on EPP, which stood up three applications plus native shells. The band spans the observed 30-40.
architect.weekly_h_why: Ongoing support while the project runs. ALL THREE recorded it at exactly 10 h/week, so the cap IS the observation and `likely` sits on it; the band is one-sided downward because nothing was ever seen above it. `weekly_cap` is enforced, so a long project does not buy proportionally more architect.
architect._disagreement: easyterms' architect figure implies 5 weeks; its retrospectives span 2026-07-21 to 2026-09-06, which is 6.9 weeks. Either roughly two weeks went unsupported or the recorded window excludes something. The fit above uses the stated 5 weeks.

standing_work._what: Work every project pays and no client document describes. THE LEAST-EVIDENCED BLOCK IN THIS MODEL, and the anchors actively exclude the work it prices: ALL THREE deferred real infrastructure. EPP's Infra-tagged stories score 0.51 points BELOW what their surface count predicts because 7.5 is marked 'seams only, IaC deferred'; its epic-6 and epic-7 retrospectives record 'no AWS resource was provisioned' and SES 'still in sandbox'; memorial-healthcare 1.4 ships CI with 'placeholder steps for EC2 deployment'. So the hours below are NOT fitted to any delivered project — they are the 2.x reasoned figures carried forward unchanged, and they are the first thing to check against a project that actually reached production. Confidence 2/10. Each item is priced through the same engine as any story, so it carries a band, a role split and a line in the feature table, and a client can argue with it item by item. Items are selected by the `stacks` list against the --stack profile; `all` means every project pays it. Suppress the section with --no-standing-work when the client is bringing an existing platform. Items carry absolute `hours` rather than a size band: a pipeline costs what it costs however the product backlog is sliced.

repo_scaffold.name: Repository scaffold and shared configuration
repo_scaffold.why: Repo or monorepo layout, shared TypeScript/lint/format config, commit hooks, the test harness everything else is written against. Generated quickly, but the decisions in it are load-bearing for every story that follows.

reasons.compressibility: The shape is conventional and generates well, but the choices are load-bearing and get read
reasons.review_tier: No money, no personal data — a spot-check of the config that ships
reasons.clarity: The stack decides it; there is nothing ambiguous left once that is chosen
reasons.hours: A day or two of decisions that everything after inherits

bmad_setup.name: BMad setup and project context
bmad_setup.why: Installing the module set, writing project-context, customising the agents to this codebase's conventions. No code is the deliverable, so nothing compresses — but it is real hours on every BMad project and pretending otherwise makes the first sprint look faster than it is.

reasons.compressibility: No code is the deliverable, so nothing compresses
reasons.review_tier: Configuration of a working process, not of anything a client depends on
reasons.novelty: Routine for a team already running BMad
reasons.hours: An afternoon of installation and project-context writing

ci_pipeline.name: Build, test and deploy pipeline
ci_pipeline.why: Pipeline per environment, caching, migrations in the deploy, preview builds. Low compressibility because the work is configuration against real systems with real credentials, and an agent cannot click through a cloud console.

reasons.compressibility: Configuration against real systems with real credentials; an agent cannot click through a cloud console
reasons.review_tier: It deploys, but it holds no data of its own
reasons.clarity: The stack and the hosting decide almost all of it
reasons.novelty: A shape the team has built before
reasons.hours: A pipeline per environment, with caching, migrations and preview builds

environments.name: Environment provisioning and secrets
environments.why: Staging and production provisioning, DNS and TLS, secret storage and rotation. Sensitive tier because a mistake here exposes production credentials, and that is read line by line before anyone signs their name to it.

reasons.compressibility: Provisioning is manual work against consoles and providers
reasons.review_tier: A mistake here exposes production credentials, so it is read line by line
reasons.clarity: The hosting choice settles the work
reasons.hours: Staging and production, with DNS, TLS and secret storage

observability.name: Logging, metrics and alerting
observability.why: Structured logs, error tracking, the handful of alerts someone will actually act on. Cheap to generate, and the first thing dropped from an estimate that has no line for it.

qa._what: qa_h as a share of the STORY-WORK TOTAL — the delivered hours of every story in the estimate. In 2.x it was a share of the manual-equivalent baseline, which is no longer computed. Re-fitted: EPP spent 40 h of QA against roughly 420 h of story work, so 0.095. n=1 AND THE OTHER TWO ANCHORS STAFFED NO QA AT ALL — memorial-healthcare and easyterms both booked zero QA hours, and memorial-healthcare is the HIPAA project. This model bills QA on every estimate because the six-role split is fixed, so on a project staffed like those two it will report hours nobody will book. Say that rather than letting it be assumed away. Confidence 4/10.

web.why: Generated E2E suites run through the bmad-qat module (https://github.com/Relevant-S/bmad-qat), plus exploratory testing and release verification. ANCHOR: EPP epics 1-9 spent 40 h of QA in total running the suite through bmad-qat, against roughly 420 h of story work — 9.5%. An estimate that assumes the tooling without naming it cannot be checked against the project that produced the rate

mobile_manual.why: Device matrix, store review cycles, and manual regression — the industry default. The 2.5x ratio to web is carried from 2.x and is not itself measured

mobile_mcp_automated.why: This company runs mobile QA through the mobile MCP server, which covers most test cases automatically. Materially cheaper than the industry default, and an estimate that ignores it is wrong in the company's disfavour

data_ml.why: Validation is empirical and iterative; correctness is statistical rather than binary

overhead_rate._what: Ceremony, demos, client communication and coordination — priced per person per week, NOT as a share of scope. UNDERIVABLE FROM THE ANCHORS: none of the three separated ceremony from delivery, so the hours below are assertions and are labelled as such. Confidence 2/10; raise it with one time-tracking export that splits meetings from build. What IS defensible is the BASIS. A status call recurs on the calendar, not on the backlog, and charged as a percentage it inherited every scope error the estimate made: a backlog counted ten times over billed ten times the meetings, which turns a granularity mistake into a commercial one. Hours are weeks x people x the rate below; the estimate still reports the implied percentage, as a cross-check rather than as the basis.

uncertainty._what: How the reported band is produced. This is the mechanism that makes false precision structurally impossible: band width is COMPUTED from the input, never chosen.
uncertainty.z_why: Multiplier on the aggregated standard deviation. 1.0 gives roughly a 68% interval, which is honest for a presale figure. Raise to 1.28 for an 80% band when a client wants more confidence — and expect a wider number.

completeness_multiplier.why: Systematic uncertainty from a thin brief is correlated risk, not independent noise, so it widens the band multiplicatively rather than being summed into the variance. At completeness 1.0 the multiplier is 1.0; at 0.5 it is about 1.7; at 0.0 it is 3.0. A two-paragraph brief therefore CANNOT produce a narrow range — the arithmetic forbids it.

uncertainty.model_risk_why: Systematic model uncertainty, as a share of the central estimate, combined in quadrature with the feature-level variance. Summing feature variances in quadrature assumes the errors are independent, and they are not: if the size-band or compression calibration is off, it is off for every feature at once. Quadrature therefore understates the real band, and understates it worst on large scopes — a hundred features would otherwise report a suspiciously tight interval. This floor represents systematic model error, which does not shrink however many features are counted. While the model is UNCALIBRATED it is set high, at 15%; est-calibrate should lower it once backtesting shows how far the model actually lands from actuals.

role_weights._what: How each component's hours divide across roles, and which roles are on the work at all. Each entry carries 'w' and optionally 'requires' (one surface) or 'requires_any' (several); a role whose surface is absent is dropped and the survivors renormalise, so the split stays an allocation of the total rather than an adjustment to it. No PM: the Architect absorbs PM responsibilities. THE ARCHITECT IS NO LONGER IN THIS TABLE except as its own component. In 2.x its hours fell out of planning_agent (0.35), planning_review (0.35) and overhead (0.40), every one of which scales with story and epic count — so a bigger backlog bought a bigger architect, which no delivered project shows. It is now `architect`, priced as setup + a capped weekly rate. The three weights it vacated were renormalised across the roles that remained. KNOWN OVER-STATEMENT, recorded rather than fixed: the six-role split is fixed by decision, and only ONE of the three anchors staffed all six. memorial-healthcare booked no QA and no DevOps; easyterms booked no BA, no UX, no QA and no DevOps, and still built a chat design system (4.1) and a WCAG-AA conformance story (4.9) with zero UX hours. On a project staffed like those two this model will report a QA and a DevOps line nobody will book. Say so rather than letting it be assumed away.

phase_map._what: Which BMad delivery phase each component is reported under. This decomposition is what makes the number legible to a client: it maps onto the process actually used rather than an invented breakdown.

calendar._what: Derived, secondary output. Hours are the deliverable; duration depends on a team shape nobody knows at presale.
calendar.hours_per_person_week_why: Six hours of focused delivery a day, five days a week. CHECKS OUT against two of the three anchors: EPP ran 690 h over 7 weeks = 98.6 h/week, and memorial-healthcare 360 h over 3.5 weeks = 102.9 h/week — both about 3.3 people at this rate. easyterms ran 240 h over 5 weeks = 48 h/week, a one-to-two person project. Confidence 6/10.
calendar.max_useful_parallelism_why: Beyond roughly six people on one workstream, coordination cost grows faster than throughput. The critical path, not the headcount, sets the floor on duration.

surfaces._what: Which kinds of work a story touches. Two jobs. It decides WHICH ROLES are on the story: a role whose `requires` surface is absent is dropped from that story's split, so a background job bills no UX and a screen bills no devops. And it is the strongest single PREDICTOR OF SIZE in the anchor — median surfaces per band across EPP's 75 stories run 1 / 2 / 3 / 3 / 4, where median acceptance-criterion count runs 5 / 7 / 8.5 / 8 / 12 and cannot tell M from L. Tagged per story at extraction. A story with no surfaces tag is treated as unknown, and unknown keeps every role in — silence must not quietly discount.
surfaces.backend: Server-side logic, data model, APIs, background jobs, third-party integrations
surfaces.frontend: Screens, client state, forms, tables — implementing a design that already exists
surfaces.design: Visual or interaction design: new screens, a design-system component, an accessibility or microcopy pass
surfaces.infra: Environments, pipelines, deployment, observability, secrets, migrations run against real systems
surfaces.data: Schema migration, import and export, backfills, reporting queries
